definition: Concerned with practical outcomes rather than abstract ideals.
example: A pragmatic timetable allowed for delays rather than assuming perfect conditions.
nuance: A pragmatic choice can be principled; the emphasis is on what works in the situation.
prompt: A team adopts a workable compromise instead of pursuing a perfect but impossible plan.
options: She took a pragmatic approach, choosing the repair they could afford today.
He was pragmatic because he followed his principles regardless of the consequences.
The proposal was pragmatic because it was explained in exceptionally clear prose.
The pragmatic manager dismissed every teammate's suggestion simply because it wasn't her own idea.
reasons: This sentence demonstrates the meaning: concerned with practical outcomes rather than abstract ideals.
Following ideals regardless of results is not evidence of practical judgment.
Clear expression is lucid; it does not establish practicality.
Rejecting ideas out of pride is stubbornness; a pragmatic person judges an idea by whether it works.

practice.prompt: A community garden has very little water during a long, dry summer.
options: The pragmatic gardener wept loudly and declared the dry summer a tragedy.
As a pragmatic gardener, she spent all summer reading soil theory and never planted a seed.
Taking a pragmatic view, the gardeners grew drought-tolerant beans instead of thirsty tomatoes.
Being pragmatic, the gardeners planted thirsty orchids simply because they found them beautiful.
reasons: Emotional theatrics are dramatic, a look-alike word; they do nothing to solve the water problem.
Studying theory without taking any action is the opposite of focusing on practical results.
Picking crops that can survive the conditions they actually face is a practical, results-minded choice.
Choosing plants for their beauty while ignoring the drought puts preference ahead of what will work.
